verbatim.text: little Tuppence can look after herself, thank you!
verbatim.purpose: Tuppence's self-mythologising catchphrase, which recurs across the book.

verbatim.text: The terms are almost too liberal, Mr. Whittington.
verbatim.purpose: Her mercenary shrewdness: she suspects the offer because of its generosity.

verbatim.text: “Jane Finn,” she said hastily; and then paused open-mouthed at the effect of those two simple words.
verbatim.purpose: The pivot of the whole novel, with its comic understatement.
An exact clue that Tuppence later recalls word for word.

verbatim.text: “No,” she replied with perfect truth. “Rita knows nothing about me.”
verbatim.purpose: Bluffing by literal truth, the chapter's comic method.

verbatim.text: “You see,” explained Tuppence still sweetly, “I’m so very fond of money!”
verbatim.purpose: States the money motif that runs through the book.
A planted clue; the clerk's name must survive exactly.

verbatim.text: “Pay the thing, will you, old bean? I’ve got nothing smaller than a five-pound note!”
verbatim.purpose: Punchline ending that the next chapter opens on.

essential: Whittington stops her in St. James's Park. She first suspects an improper approach but acquits him of that. She dislikes and distrusts him instinctively. Keep his description: big, clean-shaven, heavy jowl, small shifty cunning eyes.

He admits overhearing the Lyons' conversation and following her, gives his card (Mr. Edward Whittington, Esthonia Glassware Co., city office), and sets an eleven o'clock appointment. Tuppence accepts.
Tuppence's private resolve, ending with her catchphrase. Keep her terrier-like shake of the shoulders.
The office has a small, rather dirty outer office with a middle-aged clerk who shows her in. Do not add a telephone to the outer office.

The offer: £100 down plus expenses for a 'nominal' trip to Paris. She would enter Madame Colombier's pensionnat for possibly three months, as his ward, with no communication with friends and absolute secrecy. He suggests she pass as an American because of her slight accent picked up from an American hospital friend.

Tuppence objects that the terms are too liberal. He replies that he is paying for intelligence and for discretion not to ask questions. She insists on 'both or neither' for her partner Mr. Beresford and rises to leave.
Asked her name, she shields the archdeacon by saying 'Jane Finn', which she believes she has invented. Whittington turns purple with rage and dismay and accuses her of cat-and-mouse play.
The bluff by truthfulness: 'Rita knows nothing about me'; 'Very little indeed'; 'It might be my own name'; 'hit upon it by chance'. Show that her truthful denials increase his unease.

'How much do you want?' tempts her after a breakfast and supper of buns. She claims to live by her wits and asks for 'a little something down'. He calls it blackmail; she calls it payment for services in advance. He grudgingly admires her.

The clerk knocks and brings a 'telephone message'. Whittington frowns, says 'That'll do, Brown', abruptly dismisses her with £50 and tells her to come tomorrow. His near-genial 'au revoir' gives her a faint misgiving.
Elated, she takes a taxi to meet Tommy at the tube station and ends with the five-pound-note line.
optional: The post-office telegram to Tommy ('Don't put in advertisement') and the remark about his club subscription can be compressed to one sentence or cut. If kept, she writes it with Tommy's retained pencil.
The buns-and-reflection evening can be trimmed, but keep a one-line version of the dream of washing Esthonia Glassware that resembles hospital plates. It is a voice callback, not plot.
Her walking to the end of the street to avoid looking over-eager, and taking the stairs instead of the lift, can be cut.
Her aside that father would have a fit, and her knowing Madame Colombier's through American friends, can be shortened to one clause.
The repeated 'quit fooling' exchanges (paragraphs 91–96) can be condensed to one round. Keep 'I shouldn't like to contradict you, Mr. Whittington' if space allows.
'Life is full of surprises' can be cut if needed.

sections.name: Bluff, payment and the clerk Brown

continuity_checks: The clerk is named only in Whittington's line 'That'll do, Brown'. No narrator emphasis on it.
Tuppence never learns what Jane Finn means in this chapter, and the narration does not explain it.
Amounts are £100 offered and £50 paid, with the next appointment 'to-morrow at the same time'.
Tommy is called 'Mr. Beresford' and 'my partner'. Whittington saw them together at Lyons'.
Rita is mentioned only as an unknown name.
The chapter ends at the tube station with the five-pound-note line.
risks: The verbatim excerpts join source line breaks with single spaces, so exact-match checks should normalise whitespace.
title: MR. WHITTINGTON’S OFFER
voice_profile: Brisk, comic-thriller third person in a light, ironic 1920s register. In Tuppence's scenes the narrator sits close to her thoughts, wryly reporting her self-congratulation ('intoxicated with the success of truthfulness'), her money-mindedness and her schoolgirl slang. In Tommy's scenes the voice turns slow, practical and understated: he weighs his options, admits to nerves and feels plain indignation ('What a dirty trick!'). Comedy and menace alternate quickly. Short dialogue exchanges carry the plot. Villains give themselves away through tics: snarling, sibilance, heel-clicking. The narrator often inserts small ironic asides and callbacks such as buns, hospital plates and the terrier shake. Characters guess at identities by voice and appearance rather than knowing them.
book_context: Tommy and Tuppence are two demobilised, penniless young people who form the 'Young Adventurers, Ltd.' and blunder into a hunt for Jane Finn and a lost draft treaty. Behind the plot is the unseen 'Mr. Brown', whose rule is to stay as an unnoticed nonentity in the background. The book plants small clues that pay off later: a clerk addressed as Brown, the name Rita, a password, faces that seem familiar, the date of the 29th, a curtained recess, a portrait of the pale Russian. Ignorance is played as accidental bluff: Tuppence 'knows' only a name, and Tommy later fakes knowledge. Chapter II begins the main plot through Tuppence's chance use of 'Jane Finn'. Chapter VIII shows the conspiracy's inner council as overheard fragments, ending on a cliffhanger. Who the leaders and later-named figures are must not be revealed in these chapters.
